payload.excerpt: How to choose wedding centrepieces for your table shape, sightlines and room, then 30 ideas grouped by style, from low and tall florals to candlelit, non floral and destination tables, plus what to ask your venue and florist.
key_takeaways: Choose the centrepiece for your table shape first: one focal piece for a round table, a continuous run for a long one.
Keep arrangements low enough to talk over or lift them well clear of eye level, never in between.
Greenery, candles and repurposed ceremony flowers can carry a design further than more stems.
Ask the venue about open flame, set-up and pack-down before you fall for a design.

faq.q: How tall should wedding centrepieces be?
faq.a: Either low enough for guests to talk over or lifted well above seated eye level on a slim stand. Avoid the middle height that blocks faces across the table. Our [table decor guide](/style-advice/wedding-table-decor) covers heights in detail.

faq.q: Do long tables need one centrepiece or several?
faq.a: Several, or one continuous run. A garland, repeating low vessels or clusters of candles carry the length of a long table; a single arrangement in the middle leaves the ends bare.

faq.q: Can we reuse our ceremony flowers as centrepieces?
faq.a: Yes, if they are designed to fit the tables and someone is assigned to move them during the drinks hour. Low urns, aisle pieces and bud vases transfer most easily.

faq.q: Can we use candles at our venue?
faq.a: It depends on the venue, which sets its own rules, so ask before you design, including whether candles must sit in glass hurricanes or holders. Where open flame is restricted, battery-operated candles keep the glow.

Stems are the expensive part of most arrangements. Fewer, larger focal blooms with more foliage, candles to fill length and ceremony flowers moved to the reception all use them well. For what drives the bill, read [what drives the cost of wedding flowers](/style-advice/wedding-flowers-cost).

faq.q: What are good non floral centrepiece ideas?
faq.a: Sculptural ceramics, lanterns, mirrored plinths, fruit, books and personal objects all work. Choose one material and repeat it across the room so the tables feel designed rather than collected.
